How LLMs Shift the Center of Our Thinking

2026-10-25
  • #Product Development
  • #Generative AI
  • #Engineering Philosophy
⇄ 日本語

Now that LLMs write code, humans rarely get the chance to program anymore. I think we can now handle things like adding features, refactoring, and sometimes even investigating incidents and shipping hotfixes at a much faster pace than before.

At the same time, since LLMs started doing most of the programming, I feel that I use my head a little differently than I used to.

In this post, I want to think about where the human role has moved because of LLMs, and why programming was replaced by LLMs so quickly.

Looking back, programming was easy

Looking back, programming feels like it was largely the work of writing code that followed certain patterns. I now realize that the way I used my head back then was a little different from today, when LLMs do most of the programming and get through tasks at high speed.

Sometimes I feel that programming was, in hindsight, easy, or rather that it didn’t push my brain that hard.

I also hear people say that work has become really exhausting in the LLM era. I suspect many people share a similar feeling.

The human role has moved up one level of abstraction

So, when coding with LLMs, where does the human role lie? I think it has moved up one level of abstraction.

Sometimes the person who designs the specification and the person who implements the code are the same, but traditionally they were often separate.

For programmers, I think the main work was writing code that followed the specification.

Now, however, LLMs take care of all of that. So it may be more accurate to say that engineers now spend more time thinking from a perspective one level of abstraction higher.

In other words, the focus shifts from writing code that follows patterns to thinking through a variety of cases. For example: the scope of impact when making changes, whether something has been optimized only locally, or whether naming conventions are being violated. LLMs will investigate these things if you instruct them to, but they rarely bring them up on their own, so humans need to tell the LLM which perspectives to consider.

Putting the LLM in the position of a subordinate and giving it instructions can be seen as individuals now doing what used to be a manager’s job. And on top of that, the pace has become even faster.

Seen that way, I can sort of understand why it feels so exhausting.

Why was programming replaced so quickly?

So why was programming replaced by LLMs so suddenly? As I wrote earlier, I think it’s because programming carries a very strong sense of combining patterns and fragments.

Of course, there are people who develop with creativity, such as open-source developers. When I developed a program as open source in the past, I too had a strong sense of writing a product from scratch and testing my own ideas, thoughts, and philosophy through open source.

I do refer to existing libraries and the like, but adding originality on top of them is very hard. It’s fun, but it really does make you think, and I felt that this is where the real key lies.

Still, I continue to feel strongly that 80 to 90 percent of the programs written in ordinary work come down to combining fragments. Looking back on my past work, I feel the same way.

Building programs from past patterns, or writing programs by combining fragments, intuitively seems like something a machine could do. That’s why I think it was replaced by LLMs.

In other words, I think logic that decides the present based on past patterns will be increasingly replaced by AI such as LLMs going forward.

Problems at a higher level of abstraction can’t be replaced yet

On the other hand, problems one level of abstraction higher are often case-by-case. I think it is often difficult to derive everything from past patterns.

For example, I feel that, at this point, you can’t simply feed requests coming from upstream directly into an LLM and get a finished result. Even during implementation, if you don’t give the LLM perspectives like the ones I mentioned above, you may end up with a structure that is overly locally optimized without realizing it, and missing implementations and overlooked considerations also occur.

Over the past year, I’ve been working in an environment where I have LLMs do the coding and I write almost no code by hand. As a result, I feel that writing programs itself has been successfully replaced by LLMs.

However, going one step higher in abstraction from there, that is, grasping problems from a big-picture perspective, still feels difficult for LLMs to solve.

That is how I see things at the moment.

Conclusion

In this post, I thought about where the center of human thinking has moved now that LLMs do the programming.

Programming has a strong aspect of combining patterns and fragments, and I think that’s exactly why it was replaced by LLMs so quickly. On the other hand, problems one level of abstraction higher are case-by-case and hard to derive from past patterns, so we can’t fully leave them to LLMs yet.

I believe the key in the LLM era is to think about things from a perspective one level of abstraction higher.
